newsitem.title: Australia: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PM RULES OUT COMPENSATION FOR STOLEN GENERATION
The Prime Minister's ruled out compensation for Aborigines taken from their families, saying there'd be no end to claims against other past practices.
Opposition Leader Kim Beazley has asked Mr Howard in Parliament, why he's so hotly prepared to compensate gun-owners, but so cold to compensating black Australians who've lost their families.
Mr Howard says he continues to feel a deep personal sorrow for people who've suffered injustices under past practices.
But he says once a nation agrees to compensate for those practices, no matter how unacceptable, there would be no end to the claims or allegations made against earlier generations.
He says it would be asking one generation to accept legal responsibility for the acts of earlier generations.
Meanwhile, Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron says he'll produce the Government's formal response to a report into the forcible removal of Aboriginal children, this afternoon.
The Human Rights Commission report says the removals were genocidal and calls for reparation, including an apology and compensation.
The Government has already rejected the term "genocide" as flawed and wrong.
ABORIGINAL HEALTH GETTING SECOND CLASS STATUS: DOCTORS
A group of prominent Australian doctors and scientists says Aboriginal health is not being given the same priority as health care for white Australia.
A delegation including Australian Medical Association chief, Keith Woollard and the head of the Australian Academy of Science, Sir Gustav Nossal has met the Prime Minister to press their concerns.
Doctor Woollard says the state of Aboriginal health is a national disgrace.
He says an extra $600 million a year is needed to bring indigenous health care up to the level that would be spent on white Australians with the same level of illness.
RECONCILIATION CONVENTION ENDS
The Australian Reconciliation Convention in Melbourne has heard unless reconciliation is achieved Australia will remain a diminished nation.

Speaking on behalf of the participants at the Convention, the Chairman for the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation, Pat Dodson, has also called for the apologies of political leaders to extend to a formal apology in Parliament.

The Convention has ended with Mr Dodson calling on Australians to build a people's movement to establish a strong foundation for reconciliation, for Australia to celebrate the centenary of its nationhood in 2001.
FORMER HUMAN RIGHTS CHIEF CRITICISES GOVT
Amnesty International has launched its 1997 Refugee Campaign, with an advertising campaign aimed at making Australians realise refugees have faces and names like themselves.
Speaking at the launch, former head of the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, Justice Marcus Einfeld, criticised the Federal Government's policy on human rights.
Justice Einfeld was critical of the Government's detention of refugees when they first enter the country, and the reduction in the number of refugees accepted.
He said the reduction in the immigration rate would hurt Australia economically, and that the Government was "poll-driven" in its attitude to reconciliation with indigenous people.
HANSON HAS NEW LANDLORD
Independent MP Pauline Hanson may be looking for alternative accomodation in the near future.
The Ipswich City Council has become Miss Hanson's new landlord, after bidding three-million dollars to buy the six-storey Commonwealth Government office in Ipswich.
Councillor Paul Tully says while Ms Hanson has a three-year lease, she might be evicted when it expires.
He says the Council is proposing to use the building as its own administrative centre.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
